name: Singleton
intent: Ensure a class has only one instance and provide a global point of access to it.
whenToUse: When exactly one object must coordinate actions across the system — a shared configuration store, a connection pool, or a single logging sink. Prefer dependency injection over a hard global when testability matters.
pros: Guarantees a single instance; lazy initialization; a single, well-known access point.
cons: Introduces global state, which hides dependencies and complicates unit testing; thread-safety requires care; can mask poor cohesion.
mermaid:
classDiagram
    class Singleton {
        -instance: Singleton$
        -Singleton()
        +getInstance() Singleton$
    }
    Singleton --> Singleton : returns instance

name: Factory Method
intent: Define an interface for creating an object, but let subclasses decide which class to instantiate.
whenToUse: When a class cannot anticipate the class of objects it must create, or wants its subclasses to specify the objects it creates. Useful for decoupling construction from use.
pros: Removes new-coupling to concrete types; supports the open/closed principle; centralizes construction logic.
cons: Can require a parallel subclass hierarchy; adds indirection that may be overkill for simple cases.

name: Observer
intent: Define a one-to-many dependency so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified and updated automatically.
whenToUse: When a change to one object requires changing others and you do not know how many objects need to change — event systems, UI data binding, pub/sub within a process.
pros: Loose coupling between subject and observers; supports broadcast communication; observers can be added/removed at runtime.
cons: Notification order is unspecified; cascading updates can be hard to trace; risk of memory leaks if observers are not detached.

name: Strategy
intent: Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one, and make them interchangeable at runtime.
whenToUse: When many related classes differ only in their behavior, or you need different variants of an algorithm (sorting, pricing, routing) selectable at runtime without conditionals.
pros: Replaces conditional logic with polymorphism; algorithms vary independently of clients; easy to add new strategies.
cons: Clients must know about the different strategies; increases the number of objects; data sharing between context and strategy can be awkward.

name: Adapter
intent: Convert the interface of a class into another interface clients expect, letting classes work together that could not otherwise because of incompatible interfaces.
whenToUse: When you want to use an existing class but its interface does not match the one you need — wrapping a third-party or legacy API to fit a target contract.
pros: Reuses existing code without modifying it; separates interface conversion from business logic; supports the single-responsibility principle.
cons: Adds an extra layer of indirection; too many adapters can obscure the real structure.

name: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)
intent: Separate the write model (commands) from the read model (queries) so each can be optimized, scaled, and evolved independently.
whenToUse: When read and write workloads have very different shapes or scale — complex domains with heavy reporting, or systems that need independently scalable read replicas and denormalized read views.
pros: Independent scaling and optimization of reads vs writes; read models tailored to queries; clean separation pairs well with event sourcing.
cons: Added complexity and eventual consistency between models; more moving parts to operate; overkill for simple CRUD.
mermaid:
flowchart LR
    Client -->|Command| CommandHandler
    CommandHandler --> WriteDB[(Write Store)]
    WriteDB -->|events/sync| ReadDB[(Read Store)]
    Client -->|Query| QueryHandler
    QueryHandler --> ReadDB

name: Saga
intent: Manage a distributed transaction as a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action to undo it on failure.
whenToUse: When a business process spans multiple services and you cannot hold a single ACID transaction across them — order fulfillment, booking flows, multi-service provisioning.
pros: Avoids distributed locks; keeps each service's data local; explicit compensation makes failure handling intentional.
cons: Only eventual consistency; compensating logic is complex and error-prone; harder to reason about than a single transaction.
mermaid:
flowchart LR
    Start --> T1[Local Txn 1]
    T1 --> T2[Local Txn 2]
    T2 --> T3[Local Txn 3]
    T3 --> Done
    T3 -. on failure .-> C2[Compensate 2]
    C2 -.-> C1[Compensate 1]

name: Transactional Outbox
intent: Atomically persist domain state and the messages describing it in the same database transaction, then relay those messages to a broker asynchronously.
whenToUse: When a service must update its database AND publish an event reliably, avoiding the dual-write problem where one succeeds and the other fails.
pros: Guarantees at-least-once delivery without distributed transactions; message publication is consistent with the committed state; simple to reason about.
cons: Requires a relay/poller process; consumers must be idempotent (at-least-once); adds an outbox table and polling latency.
mermaid:
flowchart LR
    Service -->|single txn| DB[(DB + Outbox Table)]
    Relay[Outbox Relay] -->|poll| DB
    Relay -->|publish| Broker[(Message Broker)]
    Broker --> Consumer

name: Circuit Breaker
intent: Wrap calls to a remote dependency so that repeated failures trip a breaker, short-circuiting further calls until the dependency recovers.
whenToUse: When calling a remote service that may become slow or unavailable, and you want to fail fast and prevent cascading failures and resource exhaustion.
pros: Prevents cascading failures and thread/connection exhaustion; fails fast; gives the dependency time to recover; enables graceful degradation.
cons: Requires tuning thresholds and timeouts; a tripped breaker can hide transient recovery; adds state to otherwise stateless calls.
mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Closed
    Closed --> Open : failures exceed threshold
    Open --> HalfOpen : after cooldown
    HalfOpen --> Closed : trial succeeds
    HalfOpen --> Open : trial fails

name: API Gateway
intent: Provide a single entry point that routes, aggregates, and cross-cuts (auth, rate limiting, TLS) requests to a set of backend services.
whenToUse: When clients would otherwise call many microservices directly — to centralize cross-cutting concerns, simplify clients, and decouple them from internal service topology.
pros: One place for auth, rate limiting, and TLS termination; shields clients from internal topology; enables request aggregation and protocol translation.
cons: A potential single point of failure and bottleneck; can become a development chokepoint; adds an extra network hop.
mermaid:
flowchart LR
    Client --> Gateway[API Gateway]
    Gateway --> SvcA[Service A]
    Gateway --> SvcB[Service B]
    Gateway --> SvcC[Service C]
